<details class="topic-card" open>
<summary>Build a plot step by step</summary>
<div class="topic-card-body">

::: {.callout-tip}
## ggplot2 layer logic
Every plot starts with `ggplot(data, aes(...))` — this sets the data and axes.
Add layers with `+`: `geom_point()`, `geom_line()`, `labs()`, `theme_classic()`.
Order doesn't matter for most layers, but `theme_classic()` always goes last.

Need inspiration for chart types?
<ul>
  <li>General chart gallery: <a href="https://datavizproject.com/">The Data Visualization Catalogue</a></li>
  <li>R-focused chart chooser: <a href="https://www.data-to-viz.com/">From Data to Viz</a></li>
  <li>ggplot2 cheatsheet: <a href="https://rstudio.github.io/cheatsheets/html/data-visualization.html">Data visualization with ggplot2 - Cheat Sheet</a></li>
</ul>
:::

## Step 1: Start with an empty plot object
This creates a blank ggplot canvas with no data or layers.

```{webr-r}
library(tidyverse)

ggplot()
```

## Step 2: Add data and map variables to axes with `aes()`
This connects the `standards` dataset and maps concentration to x and absorbance to y.

```{webr-r}
library(tidyverse)

# Make a test data set about UV calibration standards
standards <- tibble(
  conc_ug_ml = c(0, 2.5, 5.0, 10.0, 20.0, 40.0),
  absorbance  = c(0.001, 0.112, 0.224, 0.445, 0.891, 1.782)
)

## Feed the data to ggplot and map the variables to the axes
ggplot(standards, aes(x = conc_ug_ml, y = absorbance))
```

## Step 3: Add points so the data is visible
This draws one point per observation using the x and y mappings.

```{webr-r}
library(tidyverse)

standards <- tibble(
  conc_ug_ml = c(0, 2.5, 5.0, 10.0, 20.0, 40.0),
  absorbance  = c(0.001, 0.112, 0.224, 0.445, 0.891, 1.782)
)

ggplot(standards, aes(x = conc_ug_ml, y = absorbance)) +
  geom_point(size = 2)
```

## Step 4: Add labels
This gives the plot a clear title and descriptive axis labels.

```{webr-r}
library(tidyverse)

standards <- tibble(
  conc_ug_ml = c(0, 2.5, 5.0, 10.0, 20.0, 40.0),
  absorbance  = c(0.001, 0.112, 0.224, 0.445, 0.891, 1.782)
)

ggplot(standards, aes(x = conc_ug_ml, y = absorbance)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "UV Calibration Curve — Ibuprofen",
    x     = "Concentration (µg/mL)",
    y     = "Absorbance (AU)"
  )
```

## Step 5: Apply a theme to finalize the plot
This applies `theme_classic()` to set a clean visual style.

```{webr-r}
library(tidyverse)

standards <- tibble(
  conc_ug_ml = c(0, 2.5, 5.0, 10.0, 20.0, 40.0),
  absorbance  = c(0.001, 0.112, 0.224, 0.445, 0.891, 1.782)
)

ggplot(standards, aes(x = conc_ug_ml, y = absorbance)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "UV Calibration Curve — Ibuprofen",
    x     = "Concentration (µg/mL)",
    y     = "Absorbance (AU)"
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```

</div>
</details>

<details class="topic-card">
<summary>Scatter plot</summary>
<div class="topic-card-body">

Use `geom_point()` to plot individual observations as points.

```{webr-r}
library(tidyverse)

standards <- tibble(
  conc_ug_ml = c(0, 2.5, 5.0, 10.0, 20.0, 40.0),
  absorbance  = c(0.001, 0.112, 0.224, 0.445, 0.891, 1.782)
)

ggplot(standards, aes(x = conc_ug_ml, y = absorbance)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "UV Calibration Curve — Ibuprofen",
    x     = "Concentration (µg/mL)",
    y     = "Absorbance (AU)"
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```

Add a regression line with `geom_smooth()`:

```{webr-r}
library(tidyverse)

standards <- tibble(
  conc_ug_ml = c(0, 2.5, 5.0, 10.0, 20.0, 40.0),
  absorbance  = c(0.001, 0.112, 0.224, 0.445, 0.891, 1.782)
)

ggplot(standards, aes(x = conc_ug_ml, y = absorbance)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "#3C5E3E") +
  labs(
    title = "UV Calibration Curve — Ibuprofen",
    x     = "Concentration (µg/mL)",
    y     = "Absorbance (AU)"
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```

</div>
</details>

<details class="topic-card">
<summary>Line plot</summary>
<div class="topic-card-body">

Use `geom_line()` for data over time.
Map `colour` to a grouping variable to show multiple batches.

```{webr-r}
library(tidyverse)

dissolution <- tibble(
  time_min      = rep(c(0, 15, 30, 45, 60, 90, 120), 2),
  batch         = rep(c("A", "B"), each = 7),
  pct_dissolved = c(0, 28, 52, 71, 85, 94, 98,
                    0, 22, 42, 60, 76, 89, 94)
)

ggplot(dissolution, aes(x = time_min, y = pct_dissolved, colour = batch)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(
    title  = "Dissolution Profile",
    x      = "Time (min)",
    y      = "% Dissolved",
    colour = "Batch"
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```

</div>
</details>

<details class="topic-card">
<summary>Bar chart vs. Histogram</summary>
<div class="topic-card-body">

## Bar chart
Use a bar chart `geom_col()` and `geom_errorbar()` to visualize summarized values (one value per category).

```{webr-r}
library(tidyverse)

capsules <- tibble(
  batch     = rep(c("A", "B"), each = 10),
  pct_label = c(102.8, 98.1, 101.9, 96.7, 103.5,
                99.4, 100.8, 97.3, 104.1, 101.2,
                81.7, 78.4, 83.2, 76.9, 80.5,
                79.1, 82.6, 77.8, 84.0, 80.9)
)

mean_by_batch <- capsules %>%
  group_by(batch) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_pct = mean(pct_label),
    sd_pct = sd(pct_label)
    ) %>%
  ungroup()

ggplot(mean_by_batch, aes(x = batch, y = mean_pct)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#5F7D61") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean_pct - sd_pct, ymax = mean_pct + sd_pct), width = 0.2) +
  labs(
    title = "Mean % Label Claim by Batch",
    x     = "Batch",
    y     = "Mean % Label Claim"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  theme_classic()
```

## Histogram
Use a histogram `geom_histogram()` to visualize the distribution of many raw numeric observations.

```{webr-r}
library(tidyverse)

capsules <- tibble(
  pct_label = c(99.8, 100.1, 100.3, 99.6, 100.0,
                100.2, 99.9, 100.4, 99.7, 100.1,
                100.5, 100.2, 100.7, 99.9, 100.4,
                101.0, 100.6, 100.9, 100.3, 100.8)
)

ggplot(capsules, aes(x = pct_label)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.2, fill = "#5F7D61", colour = "white") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of % Label Claim",
    x     = "% Label Claim",
    y     = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```

Difference:
<ul>
  <li>Bar chart: one bar per category, height is a known summary value.</li>
  <li>Histogram: bars represent bins of a continuous variable, showing frequency.</li>
</ul>

</div>
</details>

<details class="topic-card">
<summary>Box plot</summary>
<div class="topic-card-body">

Use `geom_boxplot()` to compare distributions across groups — ideal for batch comparisons.

How to read a boxplot:
<ul>
  <li>Center line in the box: the median (50th percentile).</li>
  <li>Bottom and top of the box: the 25th percentile (Q1) and 75th percentile (Q3).</li>
  <li>Box height: the interquartile range (IQR = Q3 - Q1), which contains the middle 50% of values.</li>
  <li>Whiskers: the most extreme values that are still within 1.5 x IQR from Q1 and Q3.</li>
  <li>Points beyond whiskers: outliers.</li>
</ul>

The example below includes a low outlier in Batch A and a high outlier in Batch B so you can see how outliers are shown.

```{webr-r}
library(tidyverse)

capsules <- tibble(
  batch     = rep(c("A", "B"), each = 10),
  pct_label = c(99.8, 100.1, 100.3, 99.6, 100.0,
                100.2, 99.9, 100.4, 99.7, 97.2,
                100.5, 100.2, 100.7, 99.9, 100.4,
                101.0, 100.6, 100.9, 100.3, 103.4)
)

ggplot(capsules, aes(x = batch, y = pct_label)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "Content Uniformity by Batch",
    x     = "Batch",
    y     = "% Label Claim"
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```

</div>
</details>

<details class="topic-card">
<summary>Color, Shape, and transparency</summary>
<div class="topic-card-body">

Color and shape can separate groups, and transparency can reveal density when points overlap.

What is transparency (`alpha`)?
<ul>
  <li>`alpha` controls how see-through a geom is.</li>
  <li>Range: `alpha = 1` means fully opaque; `alpha = 0` means fully transparent (invisible).</li>
  <li>Lower alpha values help reveal where many points overlap, because darker regions indicate higher point density.</li>
  <li>In practice, values around `0.2` to `0.5` are often useful for dense scatter or jitter plots.</li>
</ul>

Tip: If you write `geom_point(alpha = 0.3)`, all points get the same transparency.
If you map alpha inside `aes(...)`, transparency can vary by a variable.

## Use color to encode groups
Map `colour` (points/lines) or `fill` (bars/boxes) to a variable when group identity matters. Try to use color with varying brightness (e.g. one darker and one lighter) or different hues (e.g. blue vs. orange) to make groups easy to distinguish. Varying brightness is often better for colorblind accessibility than varying hue.

```{webr-r}
library(tidyverse)

dissolution <- tibble(
  time_min      = rep(c(0, 15, 30, 45, 60, 90, 120), 2),
  batch         = rep(c("A", "B"), each = 7),
  pct_dissolved = c(0, 28, 52, 71, 85, 94, 98,
                    0, 22, 42, 60, 76, 89, 94)
)

ggplot(dissolution, aes(x = time_min, y = pct_dissolved, colour = batch)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("A" = "#2F6B4F", "B" = "#D17B2D")) +
  labs(
    title  = "Color separates groups",
    x      = "Time (min)",
    y      = "% Dissolved",
    colour = "Batch"
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```

## Use color and shape to encode groups
To make your chart accessible for people with colorblindness, you can also map `shape` to a grouping variable.

```{webr-r}
library(tidyverse)

dissolution <- tibble(
  time_min      = rep(c(0, 15, 30, 45, 60, 90, 120), 2),
  batch         = rep(c("A", "B"), each = 7),
  pct_dissolved = c(0, 28, 52, 71, 85, 94, 98,
                    0, 22, 42, 60, 76, 89, 94)
)

ggplot(dissolution, aes(x = time_min, y = pct_dissolved, colour = batch, shape = batch)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("A" = "#2F6B4F", "B" = "#D17B2D")) +
labs(
  title = "Color + shape separates groups",
  x = "Time (min)",
  y = "% Dissolved",
  colour = "Batch",
  shape = "Batch"
) +
  theme_classic()
```

## Use transparency to reduce clutter
Lower `alpha` makes dense regions visible without hiding sparse points.

```{webr-r}
library(tidyverse)

set.seed(42)

dense_capsules <- tibble(
  batch = rep(c("A", "B"), each = 150),
  pct_label = c(
    rnorm(150, mean = 100.1, sd = 0.4),
    rnorm(150, mean = 98.5, sd = 0.5)
  )
)

ggplot(dense_capsules, aes(x = batch, y = pct_label, colour = batch)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.14, alpha = 0.35, size = 1.8, show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Transparency reveals point density",
    x     = "Batch",
    y     = "% Label Claim"
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```

Quick guidelines:
<ul>
  <li>Use color only when it communicates information, not decoration.</li>
  <li>Keep palettes simple and high-contrast.</li>
  <li>Use transparency when many points overlap.</li>
</ul>

</div>
</details>

<details class="topic-card">
<summary>Overplotting and how to fight it</summary>
<div class="topic-card-body">

Overplotting happens when many points overlap so heavily that patterns become hard to see.

```{webr-r}
library(tidyverse)

set.seed(42)

dense_capsules <- tibble(
  batch = rep(c("A", "B"), each = 150),
  pct_label = c(
    rnorm(150, mean = 100.1, sd = 0.4),
    rnorm(150, mean = 98.5, sd = 0.5)
  )
)

ggplot(dense_capsules, aes(x = batch, y = pct_label, colour = batch)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8, show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Overplotting",
    x = "Batch",
    y = "% Label Claim"
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```

You can fight this in many ways:

## 1) Use transparency (`alpha`)
Lower opacity reveals where points pile up.

```{webr-r}
library(tidyverse)

set.seed(42)

dense_capsules <- tibble(
  batch = rep(c("A", "B"), each = 150),
  pct_label = c(
    rnorm(150, mean = 100.1, sd = 0.4),
    rnorm(150, mean = 98.5, sd = 0.5)
  )
)

ggplot(dense_capsules, aes(x = batch, y = pct_label, colour = batch)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.15, size = 2, show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Fight overplotting with transparency",
    x = "Batch",
    y = "% Label Claim"
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```

## 2) Add jitter
Jitter spreads overlapping points so you can see repeated values.

```{webr-r}
library(tidyverse)

set.seed(42)

dense_capsules <- tibble(
  batch = rep(c("A", "B"), each = 150),
  pct_label = c(
    rnorm(150, mean = 100.1, sd = 0.4),
    rnorm(150, mean = 98.5, sd = 0.5)
  )
)

ggplot(dense_capsules, aes(x = batch, y = pct_label, colour = batch)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.45, size = 1.8, show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Fight overplotting with jitter",
    x = "Batch",
    y = "% Label Claim"
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```

## 3) Use visual abstraction
Sometimes the best fix is to summarize the data (for example with violin or box plots).
See the next collapsible section, **Visual abstraction: low to high**.

</div>
</details>

<details class="topic-card">
<summary>Visual abstraction</summary>
<div class="topic-card-body">

Visual abstraction means how much of the raw data you keep visible.
Lower abstraction shows individual observations; higher abstraction summarizes them.

## Low abstraction: points (raw observations)
You can see every data point, which makes outliers and clusters easy to spot.

```{webr-r}
library(tidyverse)

set.seed(42)

dense_capsules <- tibble(
  batch = rep(c("A", "B"), each = 150),
  pct_label = c(
    rnorm(150, mean = 100.1, sd = 0.4),
    rnorm(150, mean = 98.5, sd = 0.5)
  )
)

ggplot(dense_capsules, aes(x = batch, y = pct_label, colour = batch)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, size = 2, alpha = 0.4, show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Low abstraction: every capsule result",
    x     = "Batch",
    y     = "% Label Claim"
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```

## Medium abstraction: violin plot (distribution shape)
You lose exact points but gain a quick view of distribution shape and spread.

```{webr-r}
library(tidyverse)

set.seed(42)

dense_capsules <- tibble(
  batch = rep(c("A", "B"), each = 150),
  pct_label = c(
    rnorm(150, mean = 100.1, sd = 0.4),
    rnorm(150, mean = 98.5, sd = 0.5)
  )
)

ggplot(dense_capsules, aes(x = batch, y = pct_label, fill = batch)) +
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.7, show.legend = FALSE, colour = NA) +
  labs(
    title = "Medium abstraction: distribution by batch",
    x     = "Batch",
    y     = "% Label Claim"
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```

## High abstraction: box plot (summary statistics)
You mainly see median, quartiles, and whiskers; individual points are hidden.

```{webr-r}
library(tidyverse)

set.seed(42)

dense_capsules <- tibble(
  batch = rep(c("A", "B"), each = 150),
  pct_label = c(
    rnorm(150, mean = 100.1, sd = 0.4),
    rnorm(150, mean = 98.5, sd = 0.5)
  )
)

ggplot(dense_capsules, aes(x = batch, y = pct_label)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#5F7D61", alpha = 0.75) +
  labs(
    title = "High abstraction: summarized distribution",
    x     = "Batch",
    y     = "% Label Claim"
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```

Advantages of abstraction:
<ul>
  <li>Faster comparison across groups.</li>
  <li>Less visual clutter in large datasets.</li>
  <li>Highlights central patterns and spread.</li>
</ul>

Disadvantages of abstraction:
<ul>
  <li>Can hide outliers or multimodal patterns.</li>
  <li>Can hide sample size differences.</li>
  <li>Too much abstraction can hide important details.</li>
</ul>

</div>
</details>
